stories.title: Singapore's Stock Market Hits an All-Time High!
stories.headline_kid: While tech shares in South Korea and Taiwan came crashing down, Singapore's stock market shot up to its highest point ever!
summary: Imagine a stock market as a giant marketplace where people buy tiny pieces of companies, called shares. If a company does well, its share becomes more valuable, kind of like a trading card that becomes rare and precious.

This week, shares in South Korea and Taiwan dropped sharply. Investors got worried that companies were spending too much money on Artificial Intelligence (AI) without making enough profit back, so many people sold their shares in a hurry.

But something different happened in Singapore. Even as other markets fell, Singapore's stock market climbed to a brand-new record high! This suggests investors see Singapore as a steady, trustworthy place to keep their money, even when other markets feel shaky.

This happened while everyone was also watching America's central bank, which decided not to lower interest rates yet. Interest rates affect how expensive it is to borrow money, so people around the world pay close attention to these decisions.

lenses.me: If your parents have savings or investments linked to Singapore companies, this record high could be good news for your family's piggy bank.
lenses.family: Parents who invest through CPF or other savings plans might see their money grow a little because Singapore shares are doing well.
lenses.friends: You could chat with friends about why some countries' markets go up while others go down — it shows how connected the world's money systems are.
lenses.nation: It shows global investors trust Singapore's economy to stay stable, even when things get uncertain elsewhere in Asia.
lenses.world: It reveals how one worry — like AI spending — can shake stock markets across many countries at the same time.

stories.title: Singapore's Security Team Spots a New Online Danger Called 'Salad Bar' Extremism
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's safety officers have found people online mixing up dangerous, mismatched ideas — just like tossing random ingredients into a salad.
summary: Singapore has a team called the Internal Security Department (ISD), whose job is to spot serious dangers before they happen and keep the country safe.

Lately, ISD has noticed something new: some people online build their own strange mix of beliefs by picking bits from very different extreme groups — even groups that don't agree with each other at all! Experts call this 'salad bar' extremism, because it's like throwing random ingredients into a bowl instead of following one proper recipe.

This mixed-up thinking can be dangerous because it may push someone towards planning to hurt others. In the last 10 months, ISD has dealt with at least three such cases using a special law called the Internal Security Act, which allows them to step in early.
Instead of only punishing people, ISD also tries to help them understand why their thinking went wrong, a bit like a coach helping someone see they took a wrong turn and guiding them back on track.

lenses.me: It's a good reminder to think carefully about what you watch or read online, and to tell a trusted adult if something feels extreme or scary.
lenses.family: Parents might want to check in more with what you're watching online, similar to how some parents talk to their teens about social media use.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates can look out for each other — if a friend shares something odd or extreme, it's kind to gently ask where they learned it.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore works hard to catch dangerous online influences early, keeping everyone safer.
lenses.world: This is part of a bigger, worldwide problem — social media makes it easier than ever for extreme ideas to spread quickly.

stories.title: Japan Earthquake: Rescuers Search Mall Rubble as Deaths Rise to 13
stories.headline_kid: Rescuers are still searching for survivors after a powerful earthquake shook southern Japan, and the number of people who died has now risen to 13.
summary: A strong earthquake measuring 7.1 in magnitude — a way of measuring how powerful a quake is, where each higher number means a much stronger shake — hit southern Japan's Kyushu island on Tuesday.

The earthquake badly damaged a shopping mall and a factory. Rescuers worked through the night and the next day, pulling eight people alive out of the collapsed mall using search dogs and heavy machines.
Sadly, the death toll has now climbed to 13. The quake also knocked out power to thousands of homes and cracked open roads, making it harder for rescue teams to reach some areas.

Many Singaporean families love visiting Japan for holidays, so news like this reminds us how important it is to check travel safety advice and understand why buildings there are built to survive shaking ground.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a trip to Japan, this is a reminder to always check travel advisories before flying.
lenses.family: Parents may want to follow the news closely if they have travel plans or relatives living in Japan.
lenses.friends: You could talk with classmates about what to do if you ever feel the ground shake — staying calm and knowing where to go is important.
lenses.nation: Singapore often sends well wishes and sometimes aid to countries hit by disasters, showing regional friendship.
lenses.world: It's a reminder that earthquakes can strike suddenly, which is why many countries invest heavily in building safety standards.

stories.title: Malaysia to Send 5,000 Rohingya Refugees Back to Myanmar
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia's leader says Myanmar has agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya people, days after police detained many of them outside a refugee agency office.
summary: The Rohingya are a group of people originally from Myanmar. Many years ago, they had to flee their homes because of danger and unfair treatment, and thousands ended up living in neighbouring countries like Malaysia and Bangladesh.

This week, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced that Myanmar has agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya refugees currently in Malaysia. This came just days after Malaysian police detained more than 100 Rohingya people who had gathered outside the United Nations refugee agency's office in Kuala Lumpur.
Those detained had been evicted from their homes and were seeking help. A refugee is someone who has left their home country because it isn't safe, hoping to find shelter and safety somewhere else.
Malaysia is Singapore's closest neighbour, so how it handles situations like this can affect how countries in the region work together and support one another during difficult times.

lenses.me: It helps you understand what it means to be a refugee — someone forced to leave home because it's too dangerous to stay.
lenses.family: Your family might talk about how fortunate you are to have a safe home, and why it's important to be kind to those who don't.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with classmates how everyone deserves safety and shelter, no matter where they come from.
lenses.nation: Singapore watches how neighbouring countries handle refugee issues, since regional stability affects everyone in Southeast Asia.
lenses.world: This story is part of a much bigger, ongoing global issue — millions of people worldwide are refugees searching for a safe place to live.

stories.title: Singapore's Toh Wei Soong Wins Silver at Commonwealth Games!
stories.headline_kid: Singapore para swimmer Toh Wei Soong just won a shiny silver medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow!
summary: Toh Wei Soong, a Singaporean para swimmer, won the silver medal in the men's 50m freestyle S7 event at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 'S7' classification groups together swimmers with certain physical disabilities so competitions are fair for everyone.
He finished the race in an impressive 29.36 seconds, coming in second place at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre. A swimmer from South Africa finished just ahead of him to take the gold.
The Commonwealth Games is a big multi-sport event held every four years, where athletes from many countries — including Singapore — compete against each other in different sports.
Toh's silver medal is a proud moment for Singapore and a great example of determination, showing how hard work and belief in yourself can lead to amazing achievements.

lenses.me: His story can inspire you to keep trying your best in whatever you do, even when things feel challenging.
lenses.family: Your family might enjoy cheering for Team Singapore athletes together, especially in events like swimming.
lenses.friends: You could chat with friends about your favourite Singapore athletes and what makes their achievements special.
lenses.nation: Every medal Team Singapore wins brings pride to the whole country and encourages more young athletes to dream big.
lenses.world: Stories like his help more people around the world recognise and celebrate para-athletes' incredible abilities.
